title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 93
paragraphs: The Lydians have very nearly the same customs as the Greeks, with the exception that they prostitute their female children. They were the first of men, so far as we know, who struck and used coin of gold or silver, and also the first retailers. The Lydians themselves claim that the games now in use both among them and among the Greeks were their own invention. These games, they say, were invented among them at the same time that they colonized Tyrsenia, and this is the account they give. In the reign of Atys, son of Manes, their king, there came a grievous dearth over the whole of Lydia. The Lydians for a time continued to endure it, but afterwards, since it did not cease, they sought for remedies, and one man devised one thing and another another. Then, they say, were invented the ways of playing with dice and with knucklebones and with the ball, and all the other games except draughts, for the discovery of this last is not claimed by the Lydians. These games they invented as a resource against the famine, and this was what they would do: on one day they would play games all day in order not to feel the want of food, and on the next day they would leave off their games and eat. Thus they went on for eighteen years. Since, however, the evil did not slacken but pressed upon them ever more and more, the king divided the whole Lydian people into two parts and assigned by lot one part to remain and the other to go forth from the land. The king appointed himself to be over that part which had drawn the lot to stay in the land, and his son to be over the part that was departing, and the name of his son was Tyrsenus. So the party that had drawn the lot to leave went down to the sea at Smyrna, built ships for themselves in which they placed all the movable goods they had, and sailed away to seek means of living and a land to dwell in. After passing by many nations, they came at last to the land of the Umbrians, and there they founded cities and dwell up to the present time. And changing their name, they were called, after the king’s son who had led them out from home, not Lydians but Tyrsenians, taking the name from him.
The Lydians, then, had been made subject to the Persians, as I have said.
